name: Urticaria
description: Urticaria (hives) is characterized by the rapid onset of lesions known as wheals that consist of a central mid dermal swelling with or without surrounding erythema, with associated pruritus, lasting anywhere from 1 to 24 hours. Sheetapitta is a clinical condition characterized by the presence of elevated patches in the skin resembling that produced by the sting of the wasp, and is associated with itching (Kandu), pricking pain (Todabahulah), vomiting (Chhardi), fever (Jvara) and burning sensation (Daha). In Sheetapitta, Vata is more predominant while Udarda is a kapha dominant condition.

sections.title: Case Definition
sections.content: Urticaria (hives) is characterized by the rapid onset of lesions known as wheals that consist of a central mid dermal swelling with or without surrounding erythema, with associated pruritus, lasting anywhere from 1 to 24 hours. The term urticaria is named after the stinging nettle plant (Urtica dioica), which contains histaminic acid. Associated angioedema can sometimes be seen, characterized by swelling of the deeper dermis and subcutaneous tissue lasting up to 72 hours. Sheetapitta is a clinical condition characterized by the presence of elevated patches in the skin resembling that produced by the sting of the wasp (Varaṭīdaṣṭasaṁsthāna sotha), and is associated with itching (Kandu), pricking pain (Todabahulah), vomiting (Chhardi), fever (Jvara) and burning sensation (Daha). The term Udarda is also used to denote a similar condition. In Sheetapitta, Vata is more predominant while Udarda is a kapha dominant condition. Elevated reddish, itchy, round patches in the skin appearing in Sisira ritu, due to kapha dosha kopa is called Udarda.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Urticaria is a common skin disease. About 8–20% of individuals in the community experience an attack of urticaria at least once in their lifetime. It can be seen in all ages and sexes but is slightly more common in young adults. In 40–50% of the patients, urticaria and angioedema are seen in combination, only urticaria or angioedema is seen in 40% and 20% of the people, respectively. Urticaria is a mast cell–driven disorder characterized by the recurrent development of hives (urticaria) and/or swelling (angioedema). Urticaria affects nearly 1% of the world population, with over 100 million new cases each year. India lacks specific epidemiological studies but contributes heavily to total global burden. Chronic cases appear commonly in adults, especially women. India bears a significant burden of urticaria in absolute terms—accruing the highest number of Disability-Adjusted Life Year (DALYs) globally. In children (<14 years) at a tertiary hospital in Northern India, 57% had spontaneous urticaria; about 12% had dermographism, 2% had cold-induced, 1.3% aquagenic, and 1.7% cholinergic urticaria.

sections.title: Etiopathogenesis
sections.content: The underlying event leading to urticaria is mast cell degranulation, with release of histamine and other proinflammatory molecules. There are numerous stimuli that can lead to mast cell activation through various pathways. This release can be triggered by allergic, pseudoallergic, toxic, and physical mechanisms. Urticaria is allergic when specific antigens crosslink specific IgE antibodies attached to mast cells. Pseudoallergic urticaria describes the release of mast cell mediators after exposure to foods or medications but without the presence of specific immunoglobulin (IgE) antibodies. Endogenous or exogenous substances such as opiates, codeine, or complement proteins can alter the sensitivity of mast cells to both the stimuli. 1. Acute urticaria: The most common cause of acute urticaria is viral infections, particularly of the upper respiratory tract. Table 1: Causes of Acute Urticaria — Infections (~40%): Viral respiratory, especially rhinovirus and rotavirus (cause in 80% of children), Helicobacter pylori, Mycoplasma, hepatitis, mononucleosis, and parasitic helminths. Drugs (~10%): Beta-lactam antibiotics, NSAIDs, aspirin, ACE inhibitors, diuretics, opiates, contrast media, and blood. Foods (~1%) - Adults: Shellfish, fresh water fish, berries, nuts, peanuts, pork, chocolate, tomatoes, spices, food additives, and alcohol. Foods (~1%) - Children: Milk and other dairy products, eggs, wheat, and citrus. Inhalants: Pollens, molds, dust mites, and animal dander. Systemic diseases: Lupus erythematosus, Still's disease, thyroid disease, cryoglobulinemia, mastocytosis, and carcinomas. Emotional stress. ~50% Idiopathic. 2. Chronic urticaria: The most common underlying causes of chronic urticaria are: Autoreactivity or expression of circulating mast cell secretagogues including autoantibodies (autoimmune urticaria). This is now known as Type IIb CSU. Autoallergic Variety also known as Type I CSU. Chronic infections. Intolerance to food components. Table 2: Causes of Chronic Urticaria — Autoreactivity: Autoimmunity (anti-FcεRI-Ab, anti-IgE-Ab) (40–50%); Chronic infection: Hepatitis B, H. pylori; Intolerance: Foods, drugs, pseudoallergy; Other causes: Type I allergy, internal disease; Idiopathic ~50%. Though not all the factors listed above are seen in all cases, it must be noted that patients of CSU should NOT be subjected to detailed investigations. In majority of patients with chronic urticaria, an underlying disease will not be found.

sections.title: Ayurvedic Aetiology
sections.content: Aetiology as per Ayurveda: On exposure to cold wind, Kapha and Vata doshas get vitiated, associates with pitha dosha and causes Sheetapitta. Aaharaja hetu: i. Santarpana (Overnourishment); ii. Atilavana sevan atiamla sevan (Excessive use of salt and sour food); iii. Katu sevan, kshara sevan (Excessive use of spicy and alkaline foods); iv. Tikshna madya sevan (Excessive intake of strong alcohol); v. Viruddha aahara sevan (Intake of incompatible foods); vi. Adhyasana (Intake of food before complete digestion of earlier food); vii. Guru dravya sevan, snigdha bhojana sevan (Excessive intake of heavy and fatty meals); viii. Dadhi sevan (Excessive intake of curd); ix. Visha-yukta annapana sevan (Consumption of poisoned food articles). Viharaja hetu: i. Sheeta maruta Sparsha (Exposure to cold air); ii. Vishyukta jal snana, abhyanga, udvartana, vastra, aabhushana (Contact with poisonous substances externally for bath, massage, powder massage, clothes and ornaments); iii. Keeta damsha, bahya krimi (Insect bite, external worm infestation); iv. Chhardi nigraha, atidiwaswapna (Suppression of vomiting, excessive day sleep); v. Shishir ritu, varsha kala, diwaswapna (Day sleep in winter and rainy season). Nidanaarthakara roga: As a complication of sannipatika, pittaja, and kaphaja jwara, unmada, adhoga amlapitta. Chikitsa mithya yoga: vamana-virechana ayoga (Improperly administered purification therapies).

sections.title: Clinical Presentation
sections.content: Lesion morphology: Wheals are abrupt, well-circumscribed, raised, itchy erythematous to pale lesions varying from millimeters to several centimeters; they appear, migrate, and typically resolve within twenty-four hours without residual marks. They cause intense pruritus and/or burning sensations. Angioedema: Characterized by sudden swelling of deeper dermis, subcutaneous tissue, or mucosa (e.g., lips, eyes, genitals); often painful (not pruritic), resolving within up to 72 hours. Distribution & duration: Can affect any part of body, including scalp, palms, and soles. Associated symptoms: May include systemic manifestations like headache, dizziness, throat tightness, wheezing, GI discomfort (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea), arthralgia, fever etc. Dermographism & physical triggers: Stroking skin may reproduce wheals (dermatographism) within minutes; characteristic of physical urticaria—physical factors (pressure, temperature changes, vibration, sunlight) may precipitate symptoms. Alarming features indicating vasculitis or anaphylaxis: Wheals lasting more than 24 hours, painful, non-blanching, or leaving purpura/hyperpigmentation suggest urticarial vasculitis. Associated symptoms such as hypotension, stridor, GI symptoms, or confusion point toward systemic anaphylaxis.

sections.title: Clinical Examination
sections.content: Clinical examination of urticaria involves assessing the patient's overall health, including vital signs, identifying potential triggers (as mentioned in tables 1 & 2), and performing a physical examination of the urticarial lesions. The physical examination of urticaria includes: Type/Appearance of lesion; Size; Shape; Colour of lesion; Margin; Number; Site of lesion; Distribution—whether lesions are localized or generalized. Table 3: Classification of urticaria — Classification is based on duration and cause: Acute spontaneous urticaria (Characterized by the sudden appearance of wheals and/or angioedema lasting less than six weeks); Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) (Refers to spontaneous wheals and/or angioedema persisting for six weeks or longer. This term is interchangeable with “urticaria” or “chronic idiopathic urticaria.” There are two types Type I and Type IIb); Chronic inducible urticaria (CIndU) (Involves wheals triggered by physical stimuli (e.g., pressure, temperature changes) that continue for six weeks or more—also known as “physical urticaria.”). Summary for different types of classifications for urticaria: Acute (<6 weeks): Spontaneous (infection, allergy, idiopathic). Chronic (≥6 weeks): CSU (no trigger) and CIndU (physical/special triggers). aka CSU. Inducible Urticaria: Dermatographic, Cold, Heat, Delayed pressure, Solar, Vibratory, Aquagenic, Cholinergic, Contact, Adrenergic. Contact Urticaria: Contact with chemicals found in foods, plants, and medicines elicits urticaria. Clinical Presentation in Ayurveda: Purvarupa/ Premonitory symptoms — The premonitory symptoms of the Sheetapitta are – thirst, loss of taste, nausea, debility in the body parts, and feeling of heaviness in the body and redness of the eyes.

sections.title: Samprapti (Pathogenesis)
sections.content: Prakupita Vata and Kapha (Pradushta Kapha Maaruta) due to Sheeta Maarutadi Nidana and Sheeta Maaruta Samsparsha (exposure to cold air and objects) when being amalgamated with Pitta (Pittena Saha Sambhooya) spreads internally and externally (Bahir Antah Visarpah) and results in Sheetapitta-Udarda-Kotha. Sheetapitta Lakshana: Clinical symptoms — Table 4: Clinical Symptoms of Sheetapitta — 1. Inflammation like an insect bite; Red elevated rashes with clearly defined edges on the skin; 2. Severe itching; 3. Excessive pricking pain; 4. Vomiting; 5. Fever; 6. Burning Sensation; 7. A central wheal surrounded by an erythematous halo; 8. Flares will appear and disappear immediately. Samprapti ghataka: Dosha Tridosha; Agni Manda; Doshagati Vridhi, Tiryak, Shakha; Vyadhimarga Bahya; Dushya Rasa, Rakta; Srotas Rasavaha, Raktavaha; Sroto dushti, prakara Vimarga Gamana; Udbhava Sthana Aamashaya; Vyakti Sthana Tvak.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis
sections.content: Table 5: Differential Diagnosis of Sheetapitta — Urticarial vasculitis (Wheals lasting >24 h, often painful/burning, with residual hyperpigmentation or purpura. May present with systemic symptoms (fever, arthralgia, nephritis); biopsy shows leukocytoclastic vasculitis); Cutaneous mastocytosis (urticaria pigmentosa) (Brown/orange lesions, positive Darier's sign (wheal upon stroking), smaller fixed lesions). Bullous pemphigoid (prodromal) (Urticarial plaques evolving into tense bullae; histopathology shows subepidermal blisters with eosinophilic infiltrate). Urticarial dermatitis (Mix of urticarial wheals and eczematous patches; spongiosis and lymphocytic infiltrate on biopsy). Cutaneous lupus erythematosus (May mimic urticaria; biopsy reveals interface dermatitis, basal erythematosus vacuolization, mucin deposition). Henoch–Schönlein purpura, (IgA vasculitis), cryoglobulinemia (Purpuric vasculitis lesions, systemic signs (renal, joint, abdominal)). Fixed drug eruption (A drug reaction that occurs at the same location on skin with each exposure to a specific drug, potentially mimicking urticaria). Atopic dermatitis (It can sometimes present with urticarial appearing lesions). Insect bites (It can cause localized urticarial lesions). Pityriasis rosea (It may be mistaken for urticaria due to its appearance, but it has a characteristic herald patch and follows a specific pattern of distribution). Contact dermatitis (It can sometimes manifest as urticarial lesions, especially in irritant or allergic contact dermatitis). Sweet syndrome (Acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis) (The condition may present with urticarial lesions (oedematous, erythematous plaques that can mimic urticaria) along with fever and other systemic symptoms). Differential Diagnosis in Ayurveda: Differential diagnosis of Sheetapitta should be made from Udarda, Kotha/Utkotha, Visarpa and Kotham-Kustha. Sheetapitta is associated with picking pain and itching, aggravated at evening time. The differentiation is given as: Udarda: considered a Tridoshaja Vyadhi, Kapha produces kandu, Vata induces toda and Chardi and jvara by Pitta with Kapha predominance, distinguishing it from Sheetapitta, which has Vata-Pitta dominance. Skin eruptions look alike, but Kapha dosha is predominant; Udarda is usually aggravated at morning and sometimes it looks like skin colour. Kotha/Utkotha: features like itching and swelling are more prominent. In Kotha eruptions are numerous in number and small in size. Visarpa: Rapidly spreading skin lesions, often with systemic symptoms. Kotham-Kustha: not an acute condition- discoloration, scaling, oozing, and localized skin disease; Sheetapitta is more acute and episodic. Kotham (Kustha/skin disease, often psoriasis or eczema-like) is considered a Kapha–Pitta dominant disorder with deeper tissue involvement.

sections.title: Investigations
sections.content: Some principles that determine the investigation are: 1. Acute urticaria is generally not investigated. 2. Acute recurrent urticaria is frequently clarified with a history, as a possible trigger (food, medication, activity) can be identified. One should not forget to enquire about mucosal contacts, such as toothpaste, latex condoms, or even semen. Everything that comes in contact with the mucosa should be sought for, like drugs (prescription and over-the-counter; ask directly about aspirin and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs [NSAIDs]), all foodstuffs including spices, drinks and even chewing gum. 3. Chronic urticaria often remains idiopathic. Now there is a concept of endotypes and there are certain investigations that can be employed to differentiate the types of CSU, but they relate to the course and preferred treatment and need expert interpretation by centres that are proficient in these tests. Certain drugs like anti histamines, Omalizumab and BTK inhibitors are prescribed on the basis of these tests and endotype classification. Table 6: Investigations for Acute Urticaria — 1. Full blood count with differential white cell count; 2. CRP levels and/or ESR; 3. Culture of relevant specimens; 4. Serum allergen-specific IgE tests*; 5. Prick tests*; 6. Oral drug challenge tests. *ONLY if IgE mediated Type 1 hypersensitivity is suspected as a cause of urticaria, avoid unnecessary testing. Table 7: Investigations for Chronic spontaneous urticaria (CSU) — Differential blood count. ESR and/or CRP, Routine Tests; IgG anti-TPO and total IgE; i. Infectious diseases; ii. Thyroid Gland disorders (thyroid hormones and autoantibodies); iii. Concomitant CIndU (see below); iv. Severe systemic diseases (e.g. tryptase); v. Other (e.g. lesional skin biopsy). For identification of underlying causes or eliciting factors and for ruling out possible differential diagnoses if indicated based on history. Table 8: Investigations for Chronic inducible urticaria (CIndU) — Challenge test/ Type Challenge test; Provocative test: Cold Urticaria (Apply cold stimulus (e.g. ice cube on forearm) and observe for wheal-and-flare reaction during skin rewarming); Heat urticaria (Heat provocation and threshold test); Solar urticaria (Photo Test to various wavelengths of light); Symptomatic dermatographism (Stroke skin with firm object (e.g. tongue blade or other instrument with a firm edge), or a dermographometer); Cholinergic urticaria (Provocative challenges that increase body temperature (e.g, exercise, hot water immersion)).

sections.title: Diagnostic Criteria
sections.content: The diagnosis will be done based upon the clinical presentation, clinical examination and investigations as mentioned above. Ayurvedic Diagnostic Approach: Nidana (Etiological Factors): Includes exposure to cold breeze, incompatible foods (Viruddha Ahara), and seasonal triggers. Dosha Assessment: Predominant involvement of Vata and Pitta with Rakta and Rasa as affected dhatus. Twak Vikara Evaluation: Observation of skin lesions, itching (Kandu), burning sensation (Daha), and swelling (Shotha). Rogabala and Vyadhibala: Strength of the disease and the patient's immunity are considered for treatment planning.

sections.title: Principles of Management
sections.content: The principles of management include assessment of signs and symptoms before initiating treatment and the need for management through conventional treatment for associated comorbidities. If the patient is already under standard care, the physician may advice to continue the same along with add-on Ayurvedic treatment and can be assessed for the same in the follow ups for tapering or discontinue the treatment in consultation with the conventional physician. Red Flag Signs: These signs should be assessed before initiating treatment for need for management/consultation through modern medicine: Angioedema of airway structures & family History; Respiratory distress (stridor, wheezing); Cardiovascular signs (hypotension, tachycardia, syncope); Hives that persist > 24–48 hours or ulcerate; Systemic signs (fever, weight loss, night sweats, arthralgia). Chronic hives (> 6 weeks); Urticaria as a part of severe allergic reaction; Urticaria with symptoms of anaphylaxis (dizziness, breathing troubles and swelling of tongue, lips, mouth or throat).

sections.title: Preventive Treatment
sections.content: (A) Prevention Management: Hydration: Maintain adequate water intake to support skin hydration and overall health. Avoid known triggers. (Nidana Parivarjan). Regular moderate exercise: Promotes immune balance. Sleep and environmental controls: Ensure proper sleep hygiene; maintain cool, well-ventilated surroundings; choose breathable, loose cotton clothing. Bath and change of clothes: If pollen or animal contact has triggered urticaria in the past, take a bath and change clothes. Yoga: Regular practice of yogic techniques such as Neti (nasal cleansing), selected Asanas—including Tadasana (Palm Tree Pose), Trikonasana (Triangle Pose), Veerabhadrasana I & II (Warrior Poses I & II), Setu Bandhasana (Bridge Pose), and Shavasana (Corpse Pose)—along with breathing practices (Pranayama) such as Nadi Shodhana (alternate nostril breathing), Bhramari (humming bee breathing), and Sheetali (cooling breath), play a significant role in maintaining overall health. These practices collectively help in reducing psychological stress, improving blood circulation, facilitating detoxification, and regulating immune function. Furthermore, the inclusion of Dhyana (meditation) and Yoga Nidra (yogic relaxation) enhances mental stability and promotes psychosomatic balance. Together, these interventions contribute to strengthening the body's natural defense mechanisms and may aid in reducing the risk or progression of disorders such as Urticaria.

sections.title: Treatment Levels
sections.content: (B) Curative Interventions: Line of treatment: The treatment of Sheetapitta is based on the doshagati and includes Shamana, shodhana, and Bahi Parimarjana Chikitsa. Krimighna and Dadrughna drugs can also be added subject to involvement of dosha and the line of treatment is similar to that of Kushtha, Amlapitta and Udarda. Internal Medications — Table 9: Internal Medications for Sheetapitta — Haridra khand (Churna 5-10 Gms, BD (A/F), One month, Milk); Nimbadi Churna (Churna 3-5 Gms, BD (A/F), One month, Water); Triphala Churna (Churna 3-5 Gms, BD (A/F), One month, Water); Guduchi (Tinospora cordifolia) (Churna 3-5 Gms, BD (A/F), One month, Water); Eladi Churna (Churna 3-5 Gms, BD (A/F), One month, Water); Shudh Gairik (Churna 250 mg, BD (A/F), 15 days, Honey or cold water); Shankh bhasma (Bhasma 250 mg, BD (A/F), 15 days, Honey or cold water); Muktashukti Bhasma (Bhasma 250-500 mg, BD (A/F), 15 days, Water); Duralabadi kashayam (Decoction 25-50 ml, BD (A/F), One month, NA); Panchatikta Kashaya (Decoction 25-50 ml, BD (A/F), One month, NA); Ushirasav (Liquid 20 ml with equal water, BD (A/F), One month, water); Sutashekara ras (Tablet 250-500 mg, BD (A/F), 15 days, Sita yukta Dugdha); Gandhaka Rasayana (Tablet 250-500 mg, BD (A/F), 15 days, Milk); Arogyavardhini Vati (Tablet 250-500 mg, BD (A/F), 15 days, Water); Sheetapitta bhanjani ras (Tablet 125-250 mg, BD (A/F), 15 days, Ghee or Honey); Kamadudha rasa (Tablet 250 mg, BD (A/F), 15 days, Sita or Jiraka); Chandrakala Rasa (Tablet 250 mg, BD (A/F), 15 days, Cow's milk, sugar, or honey); Krimimudgara rasa (Tablet 250mg, BD (A/F), 15 days, Water). External Applications — Nimbadi taila (Taila QS, As per requirement, 15 days); Eladi taila (Taila QS, As per requirement, 15 days); Karanja taila (Taila QS, As per requirement, 15 days). Table 10: Pathya-Apathya (Do's & Don'ts) for Sheetapitta — Pathya/Do's: Jeerna Shali (Old Rice); Jangala Mamsa (meat from animals of arid or dry regions); Triphala; Madhu (Honey); Mudga Yusha (Green Gram Soup); Kulattha Yusha (Horse Gram Soup); Ushnodaka (Luke warm Water); Karavellaka Shaka (Bitter Gourd Vegetable); Moolaka Yusha (Radish Soup); Dadima Phala (Pomegranate); Shigru Shaka (Drumstick leaves); Moolaka Shaka (Radish leafy vegetable); Kashaya Rasa (Astringent Taste). Apathya/Don'ts: Ksheera vikarani (milk products); Ikshu Vikarani (sugarcane products); Matsya (Fish); Anupa-Audaka Mamsa (Meat from aquatic or marsh-dwelling animals); Naveena Madhya (Freshly prepared alcoholic beverage); Virudhahara (incompatible food); Snigdha (Oily foods), Amla (Sour Foods), Madhura (Sweets), lavana (Saltish Foods); Guru Annapana (heavy to digest food). Vihara-Apathya: Divaswapna (Day Sleep); Poorva and Daksheena Disha Pavana (Eastern and Southern directional winds); Atapa Sevana (Sun Exposure); Vyavaya (Sexual Activity); Snana (Bathing). AT LEVEL 1- Solo Physician Clinic/ Health & Health Clinic/ PHC: Clinical diagnosis: Sheetpitta/Urticaria is diagnosed after a complete medical history, psychiatric, triggering factors and physical examination. Some investigations, like CBC, ESR, CRP, Stool Examination, total IgE may also be done. Management: 1. Nidana parivarjan: Nidana Parivarjana is the primary line of treatment for Sheetpitta; therefore, it is advised to identify the causative factors and avoid them as much as possible. 2. Chikitsa: Internal Medications — Table 11: Medications for Level 1 — Haridrakhanda (Powder 3-5 Gms, BD (A/F), 15 days, Milk); Yavanyadi choornam (Powder 3-5 Gms, BD (A/F), 15 days, Water); Sheetapitta bhanjana ras (Tablet 200 mg, BD (A/F), 15 days, Honey); Sutasekhara rasa (Tablet 300 mg, BD (A/F), 15 days, Honey); Gandhaka Powder (Powder 250-500, BD (A/F), 15 days, Milk); Duralabhadi Kashayam (Decoction 25-50 ml, OD (E/S), 15 days, Warm water); Patola Katurohinyadi Kashayam (Decoction 25-50 ml, OD (E/S), 15 days, Warm water); Bilvadi Gutika (Tablet 250-500 mg, BD (A/F), 15 days, Luke Water). Bahir Parimarjana Chikitsa — Durvadya Taila (Taila QS, As per requirement, 15 days); Brihat marichyadi Tailam (QS, As per requirement, 15 days); Nimbadi tailam (Taila QS, As per requirement, 15 days). FollowUp: In the first-level management of Sheetapitta, which primarily involves Nidana Parivarjana (avoiding causative factors), intake of shamanoushadhis and dietary regulation, the follow-up period is relatively short and focused on early symptom resolution and prevention of escalation. Initial Phase (Days 1–7): Frequency: Every 3–5 days; Purpose: Monitor response to initial interventions; Focus: Reduction in itching (Kandu), swelling (Shotha), and redness (Raga). Stabilization Phase (Weeks 2–4): Frequency: Weekly; Purpose: Ensure sustained relief and prevent recurrence; Focus: Evaluate digestion (Agni), skin condition, and adherence to Pathya-Apathya guidelines. Transition Criteria to Second-Level: If symptoms persist beyond 2–3 weeks or recur after initial relief or new symptoms like Daha, Jwara, or Chhardi appears, the patient may be referred to level 2. Referral Criteria: If symptoms cannot be controlled with regular treatment and even after avoidance of triggering factors; Patients suffering from angioedema; Substantial impact on their quality of life and activities of daily living; Evidence of an increase in severity/complications; Diagnostic uncertainty; Uncontrolled comorbidities such as diabetes mellitus, hypertension etc.; Urticaria with symptoms of anaphylaxis; Hereditary angioedema, physical urticaria not responding to treatment. AT LEVEL 2: (CHC/Small hospitals (10-20 bedded hospitals with basic facilities such as routine investigations, X-ray). Clinical Diagnosis: Same as Level 1. Non-responding cases of mild to moderate severity and severe cases shall be referred to level 2 and 3. The case referred from Level 1, or a fresh case must be evaluated thoroughly for any complications. Identification of patient specific etiopathological factors (nidana), dosha involvement (Initial kapha-vata dominance may start showing signs of Pitta aggravation) and assessment of Rogibala is needed before initiation of treatment. Investigations: The diagnosis would be primarily clinical. Investigations may be necessary (if not done at primary level) to investigate complications or exclude other differential diagnoses as follows: Infection screens; Thyroid Panels. Management: The second level management of Sheetapitta includes Shamana as well as Shodhana Chikitsa—a purificatory approach used when symptoms are chronic, recurrent, or associated with Bahudosha Avastha (excessive doshic aggravation). Purification/other procedures: 1. Vamana (Therapeutic Emesis): Decoctions of Patola, Nimba, Vaca used for emesis; Eliminates Kapha and Ama from the Amasaya; Indicated when itching and swelling are predominant. 2. Virechana (Purgation Therapy): Triphala Churna, Trivrit Avaleha, Navakarshika Kashaya; Targets Pitta and Rakta Dushti; Especially useful when burning sensation (Daha) and redness (Raga) are prominent. Recommended Follow-Up Period: Immediate Post-Shodhana Phase (Days 1–7): Frequency: Daily or alternate days; Focus: Monitor Samyak Lakshana (signs of proper purification), bowel movements, hydration, and vitals; Care: Begin Samsarjana Krama (gradual diet restoration) with Manda, Peya, Vilepi. Recovery Phase (Weeks 2–4): Frequency: Weekly; Focus: Assess reduction in symptoms like Kandu, Daha, Shotha; Care: Introduce Shamana Chikitsa if needed, continue dietary regulation. Maintenance Phase (Weeks 5–12): Frequency: Biweekly to monthly; Focus: Prevent recurrence, monitor Agni, Bala, and skin health; Care: Use Rasayana therapy (e.g. Haridrakhand, Guduchi, Triphala) to rebuild immunity. Referral Criteria: Same as mentioned earlier at Level 1; Failure to respond to initial medical management/ Acute exacerbation of the disease; Hereditary angioedema; Physical urticaria not responding to therapy; Any other life-threatening complications; Clinical diagnosis referral from second-level to third-level is considered when symptoms intensify or become chronic, requiring deeper detoxification. AT LEVEL 3: (Ayush hospitals attached with teaching Institution, District Level/ Integrated/ State Ayush Hospitals). Clinical Diagnosis: Same as Levels 1 & 2. Confirm diagnosis and severity with the help of following investigations: Screening for neutrophil rich infiltrates in skin biopsy, performing gene mutation analysis for hereditary periodic fever syndromes; Autologous Serum Skin Test (ASST); In cases of suspected hereditary angioedema (HAE), test for complement C4 levels; If mean wheal duration >24 hours, perform biopsy of skin lesion to assess for signs of urticarial vasculitis; Complement activity tests; Anti-nuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and/or anti-citrullinated protein; Thyroid autoantibodies to TSH receptor, thyroglobulin, thyroid peroxidase and sodium/iodine symporter; Biopsy to be done when there is doubt regarding the diagnosis (lesions persisting beyond 24 hrs, non-blanchable, fever, joint pains etc.); This level is applied when the disease is chronic or relapsing and there is significant doshic involvement (especially Pitta and Rakta). Management: The third-level management of Sheetapitta includes raktamoksha along with other sodhana therapies. Medical management with the following regimes can be given if there is pitha involvement. Sanskrit verse quoted. 1. Triphala + honey: Pitta hara and doshasamaka. 2. Navakarshika Guggulu. Table 12: Internal Medications for Level 3 — Haridrakhanda (Powder 5-10 gms, After food, Two times a day, Luke warm Water); Durva, Haridra Kalka (kalka lepa, Sufficient, Two times a day); Seetapitta bhanjan ras (Tablet 125 mg, After food, Two times a day, Honey); Laghumalini Vasanta Rasa (Tablet 125 mg-250mg, After food, Two times a day); Laghu Sutashekhara Rasa (Tablet 250mg-500mg, After food, Two times a day); Ardraka Swarasa (15-24 ml, After food, Two times a day, Purana guda). Purification/other procedures: Vamana and Virechana therapies as mentioned in level 1 and 2; Raktamokshana (Bloodletting) - Siravyadha or Jalaukavacharana (leech therapy) - Applied when symptoms are localized and severe; Helps purify Rakta Dhatu and reduce inflammation. Follow Up: Immediate Post-Shodhana Phase (Days 1–7): Frequency: Daily or alternate days; Focus: Monitor Samyak Lakshana (signs of proper purification), bowel movements, hydration, and vitals; Care: Begin samsarjana krama (gradual diet restoration) with Manda, Peya, Vilepi. Recovery Phase (Weeks 2–4): Frequency: Weekly; Focus: Assess reduction in symptoms like Kandu, Daha, Shotha; Care: Introduce Shamana Chikitsa if needed, continue dietary regulation. Maintenance Phase (Weeks 5–12): Frequency: Biweekly to monthly; Focus: Prevent recurrence, monitor Agni, Bala, and skin health; Care: Use Rasayana therapy (e.g., Haridrakhand, Guduchi, Triphala) to build immunity. Referral Criteria: Same as mentioned earlier at Level 1 & 2; Other modalities can be considered depending on the case.

sections.title: Clinical Algorithm
sections.content: Annexure I: Algorithm of Treatment Process for Sheetapitta (Urticaria): Initial Clinical Evaluation → Patient Presents with Sheetapitta (Inflammation like an insect bite; Red elevated rashes with clearly defined edges on the skin + a central wheal surrounded by an erythematous halo) → Diagnosis through clinical signs & symptoms — Nidana (Etiological Factors): Includes exposure to cold breeze, incompatible foods (Viruddha Ahara), and seasonal triggers. Dosha Assessment: Predominant involvement of Vata and Pitta with Rakta and Rasa as affected dhatus. Twak Vikara Evaluation: Observation of skin lesions, itching (Kandu), burning sensation (Daha), and swelling (Shotha). Rogabala and Vyadhibala: Strength of the disease and the patient's immunity are considered for treatment planning. Basic Labs: CBC, ESR, CRP, Stool examination, Provocative tests, Total IgE → Non-responding cases of mild to moderate severity and severe cases shall be referred to level 2. At level 1, management of Sheetapitta primarily involves Nidana Parivarjana (avoiding causative factors), Shamana Chikitsa and Pathyaseelana → The second level management of Sheetapitta includes Shamana as well as Shodhana Chikitsa—a purificatory approach used when symptoms are chronic, recurrent, or associated with Bahudosha Avastha (excessive doshic aggravation). → If improvement is not noted, re-assessment at level 3. This level is applied when the disease is chronic or relapsing and there is significant doshic involvement (especially Pitta and Rakta). The third-level management of Sheetapitta also includes Raktamoksha along with other sodhana therapies. Red Flag Signs: Angioedema of airway structures; Respiratory distress (stridor, wheezing); Cardiovascular signs (hypotension, tachycardia, syncope); Hives that persist > 24–48 hours or ulcerate; Systemic signs (fever, weight loss, night sweats, arthralgia); Chronic hives (> 6 weeks). AUXILIARY MEASURES: Diet: Laghu anna (Light food), Tikta shaka (green leafy vegetables), Ghrita (Ghrita), Mudga (Green gram), Aadaki (Pigeon pea), Masoora (Red lentil), yava (barley), Godhooma (wheat), Madhu (Honey), Sali ( Rice), Karkati (Cucumber), Triphala, Patola (Snake gourd), Kakamachi (Black night shade), Nimbapatra (Neem leaves), Lasuna (garlic), Punarnava (spreading hogweed), Khadira (Black catechu), Tila Taila (gingelly oil). Lifestyle: Avoid triggers: cold exposure, spicy and sour foods, and allergens. Favor warm, light, and easily digestible foods. Long-term immune support with Rasayana therapy (e.g., Chyawanprash, Amalaki Rasayana). Yoga: Practice stress-reducing techniques: Yoga, meditation.

sections.title: General Instructions
sections.content: Avoid known triggers (Nidana Parivarjan). Maintain adequate hydration. Regular moderate exercise promotes immune balance. Ensure proper sleep hygiene; maintain cool, well-ventilated surroundings; choose breathable, loose cotton clothing. If pollen or animal contact has triggered urticaria in the past, take a bath and change clothes.
